tagline: Draw, handle, and process blood specimens safely and accurately.

domains.name: Safety and Compliance
domains.description: Workplace safety, infection control, PHI, and quality control.

domains.name: Patient Preparation
domains.description: Communication, identification, consent, and order verification.

domains.name: Routine Blood Collections
domains.description: Venipuncture and capillary collection technique and complications.

domains.name: Special Collections
domains.description: Blood cultures, point-of-care testing, and specialized samples.

domains.name: Processing
domains.description: Specimen preparation, integrity, chain of custody, and reporting.

questions.stem: Immediately after completing a venipuncture, what should the phlebotomist do with the used needle?

options.text: Recap the needle with two hands, then place it in the regular trash
Activate the safety device and drop it into the sharps container without recapping
Bend the needle to make it unusable before disposal
Set it on the tray until all tubes are labeled, then discard it

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** OSHA requires engaging the engineered safety feature and disposing of the needle in a puncture-resistant sharps container at the point of use, without recapping. Why the others are wrong: **A** two-handed recapping is prohibited because it greatly raises needlestick risk, and sharps never go in regular trash; **C** bending or breaking needles is banned for the same reason; **D** leaving an exposed needle on the tray creates an injury hazard for the worker and others.

questions.stem: A phlebotomist sustains a needlestick from a contaminated needle while drawing a patient. After washing the site, what is the next appropriate step?

options.text: Squeeze the wound hard for several minutes to force out any blood
Finish the shift and report the incident only if symptoms develop
Report the exposure to a supervisor and follow the facility's post-exposure protocol
Apply a topical antibiotic and continue working without notifying anyone

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** After washing with soap and water, the exposed worker must immediately report to a supervisor so the facility's bloodborne-pathogen post-exposure follow-up (evaluation, source testing, prophylaxis) can begin promptly. Why the others are wrong: **B** delaying report can forfeit time-sensitive prophylaxis and is a violation of the exposure-control plan; **A** vigorous squeezing is not recommended and may traumatize tissue without proven benefit; **D** self-treating and staying quiet bypasses mandated medical evaluation and documentation.

questions.stem: Under OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, which two protections must the employer provide to phlebotomists? (Select two.)

options.text: A written exposure-control plan that is reviewed and updated
Personal protective equipment at no cost to the employee
A guarantee that no employee will ever be exposed
Permission to reuse single-use sharps to reduce waste

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard requires employers to maintain a written, regularly updated exposure-control plan and to furnish appropriate PPE at no cost to workers. Why the others are wrong: **C** OSHA mandates risk-reduction measures but cannot guarantee zero exposure; **D** reusing single-use sharps is prohibited because it dramatically increases injury and infection risk.

questions.stem: What is the single most effective measure for preventing the transmission of infection between patients in the healthcare setting?

options.text: Cleaning the venipuncture site with alcohol
Wearing a gown for every blood draw
Using a fresh tourniquet stored in a sealed bag
Performing hand hygiene before and after every patient contact

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Hand hygiene (washing or alcohol-based rub) before and after each patient is recognized by the CDC as the single most important action to prevent healthcare-associated infection transmission. Why the others are wrong: **B** a gown is used only when contamination of clothing is anticipated, not routinely for every draw; **C** tourniquet handling matters but is secondary to hand hygiene; **A** site antisepsis protects that one puncture but does not prevent transfer of organisms from patient to patient.

questions.stem: A patient is on contact precautions for a multidrug-resistant organism. Which PPE is minimally required before the phlebotomist enters the room to draw blood?

options.text: Gloves and a gown
Gloves and an N95 respirator
A surgical mask and eye protection only
Gloves only

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Contact precautions require donning gloves and a gown before entering the room to prevent transfer of organisms spread by direct or indirect contact. Why the others are wrong: **B** an N95 respirator is for airborne precautions (e.g., tuberculosis), not contact precautions; **C** a mask and eye protection address droplet/spray exposure, not contact transmission; **D** gloves alone omit the required gown that protects clothing from contaminated surfaces.

questions.stem: When donning personal protective equipment to enter an isolation room, in what order should the items be put on?

options.text: Mask, gloves, gown, goggles
Gloves, gown, mask, goggles
Gown, mask, goggles, gloves
Goggles, gloves, gown, mask

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The CDC donning sequence is gown first, then mask/respirator, then goggles or face shield, and finally gloves, which are pulled over the gown cuffs. Why the others are wrong: **B** putting gloves on first leaves them contaminated while handling the gown and prevents covering the cuffs; **A** donning gloves before the gown breaks the protective layering; **D** starting with goggles and gloves disrupts the established sequence and leaves cuffs exposed.

questions.stem: Under HIPAA, a phlebotomist may share a patient's protected health information without specific authorization in which situation?

options.text: On a personal social media account, omitting only the patient's last name
With a coworker who is simply curious about the patient's diagnosis
With the patient's employer upon the employer's request
With the laboratory and ordering provider for the patient's treatment and testing

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** HIPAA permits disclosure of PHI without separate authorization for treatment, payment, and healthcare operations, so sharing results with the lab and ordering provider is allowed. Why the others are wrong: **B** disclosing to a curious coworker has no treatment purpose and violates minimum-necessary access; **C** an employer is not entitled to results without the patient's authorization; **A** posting any identifiable detail on social media is a serious breach regardless of which fields are omitted.

questions.stem: A patient asks the phlebotomist, "What does this test for, and do you think something is wrong with me?" The phlebotomist is not qualified to interpret results. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Offer a likely diagnosis based on the tests ordered
Explain that interpreting results is outside a phlebotomist's scope and refer the patient to the ordering provider
Tell the patient the results are confidential and refuse to say anything further
Reassure the patient that the results are probably normal

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Diagnosing or interpreting results is outside a phlebotomist's scope of practice; the proper action is to acknowledge the question and refer the patient to the provider who can interpret findings. Why the others are wrong: **A** suggesting a diagnosis exceeds scope and may be inaccurate and harmful; **C** a curt refusal is poor communication and does not direct the patient to a proper resource; **D** predicting results gives false reassurance the phlebotomist is not qualified to provide.

questions.stem: A small blood spill occurs on the counter. After absorbing the spill, which agent is appropriate for decontaminating the surface?

options.text: A 1:10 dilution of household bleach (sodium hypochlorite) or an EPA-registered tuberculocidal disinfectant
70% isopropyl alcohol applied once
Plain soap and warm water
A dry paper towel wipe followed by air drying

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A 1:10 bleach solution (or an EPA-registered tuberculocidal/intermediate-level disinfectant) is the standard for decontaminating blood spills because it reliably inactivates bloodborne pathogens. Why the others are wrong: **B** 70% alcohol is used for skin antisepsis, not for blood-spill surface decontamination; **C** soap and water cleans but does not adequately disinfect a biohazard spill; **D** a dry wipe neither contains nor disinfects the spill and can aerosolize contaminants.

questions.stem: Which two practices are components of Standard Precautions, which apply to every patient regardless of diagnosis? (Select two.)

options.text: Performing hand hygiene before and after patient contact
Treating all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious
Wearing an N95 respirator for every patient encounter
Placing every patient in a negative-pressure room

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Standard Precautions assume that any patient's blood and body fluids may be infectious and require hand hygiene with every contact, applied universally. Why the others are wrong: **C** an N95 respirator is reserved for airborne precautions, not routine encounters; **D** negative-pressure isolation is an airborne-precaution measure, not a universal standard for every patient.

questions.stem: A glucose meter used for point-of-care testing must have its quality-control (QC) solutions run according to the manufacturer's instructions. Why is running QC important?

options.text: It replaces the need to check reagent expiration dates
It calibrates the patient's blood glucose to a fasting baseline
It satisfies HIPAA documentation requirements for the patient
It verifies that the instrument and reagents are performing accurately before patient results are reported

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Running control solutions confirms the analyzer and reagents are within acceptable limits, so reported patient results can be trusted. Why the others are wrong: **B** QC checks the device, not the patient's physiologic baseline; **C** QC is a CLIA quality requirement, not a HIPAA privacy requirement; **A** QC and expiration checks are both required and one does not replace the other.

questions.stem: What does the biohazard symbol on a container or door primarily communicate to healthcare workers?

options.text: The container holds radioactive specimens only
The contents or area may contain infectious materials requiring special handling
The materials inside are chemically flammable
The container is approved for regular household trash

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The biohazard symbol warns that infectious or potentially infectious biological materials are present and must be handled and disposed of with appropriate precautions. Why the others are wrong: **A** radioactive hazards use a distinct radiation trefoil symbol; **C** flammability is indicated by chemical/fire hazard labeling, not the biohazard sign; **D** the symbol specifically signals regulated medical waste, the opposite of ordinary trash.

questions.stem: What is the correct way to verify the identity of an alert, adult inpatient before drawing blood?

options.text: Confirm the room and bed number match the requisition
Read the patient's name aloud and proceed when they nod
Ask the patient to state their full name and date of birth, then match them to the requisition and wristband
Ask a family member at the bedside to confirm the patient's name

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Identity must be confirmed with at least two patient-specific identifiers, obtained by having the patient actively state name and date of birth and matching them to the requisition and wristband. Why the others are wrong: **B** reading the name aloud lets a confused or drowsy patient agree to the wrong name; **A** room and bed numbers are not patient identifiers because patients move; **D** relying on a family member instead of the patient and wristband does not meet the active two-identifier standard.

questions.stem: A requisition orders a fasting blood glucose. The patient reports eating breakfast two hours ago. What is the best action?

options.text: Notify the nurse or ordering provider and document the non-fasting status before proceeding as directed
Draw the specimen and report it as a fasting glucose anyway
Refuse to draw and send the patient home
Wait 30 minutes and then draw, treating it as fasting

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The phlebotomist should alert the nurse or provider and document the non-fasting status so the order can be confirmed or rescheduled, preserving result accuracy. Why the others are wrong: **B** labeling a non-fasting specimen as fasting falsifies the record and misleads interpretation; **C** unilaterally sending the patient home exceeds the phlebotomist's authority; **D** two hours post-meal is not a true fast, so a short wait does not make the result fasting.

questions.stem: An outpatient becomes upset and says, "I changed my mind, I don't want my blood drawn." The phlebotomist had already applied the tourniquet. What should the phlebotomist do?

options.text: Proceed quickly because consent was implied when the patient sat down
Stop, remove the tourniquet, and respect the patient's right to refuse, then notify the provider
Insist the test is necessary and continue the draw
Restrain the arm gently and complete the venipuncture

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A competent patient can withdraw consent at any time; the phlebotomist must stop, remove the tourniquet, and inform the provider rather than continue. Why the others are wrong: **A** prior implied consent does not override an explicit, current refusal; **C** pressuring the patient to continue ignores their autonomy; **D** restraining the arm to complete the draw constitutes battery.

questions.stem: A patient who speaks limited English looks confused about the procedure. What is the most appropriate way to obtain understanding and cooperation?

options.text: Skip the explanation and proceed since the order is valid
Speak louder and use the same English words
Arrange for a qualified medical interpreter to explain the procedure
Ask another waiting patient to translate

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Using a qualified medical interpreter ensures accurate, confidential communication and supports informed cooperation across a language barrier. Why the others are wrong: **B** raising volume does not overcome a language difference; **A** omitting any explanation undermines understanding and the patient's right to be informed; **D** an untrained bystander cannot ensure accuracy and breaches confidentiality.

questions.stem: A patient has an IV running in the left arm and a healed mastectomy with lymph node removal on the right side. From where should routine venipuncture be performed?

options.text: From either antecubital fossa since both are acceptable
From the right arm because it has no IV
From the left arm directly above the running IV
Below the IV site is avoided and the mastectomy side is avoided, so an alternative site such as a hand vein is selected after consulting the patient's nurse

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Both standard antecubital sites are compromised, so the phlebotomist avoids the mastectomy side (lymphedema risk) and the IV arm, and selects an alternative such as a hand vein, consulting nursing as needed. Why the others are wrong: **B** the right arm is the mastectomy side and is avoided due to impaired lymph drainage and infection risk; **C** drawing above a running IV contaminates the specimen with IV fluid; **A** neither antecubital fossa is acceptable here given the IV and mastectomy.

questions.stem: Before an outpatient venipuncture, how should the phlebotomist position a patient who has fainted during previous blood draws?

options.text: Seated in a chair with armrests or lying down, so the patient cannot fall if syncope occurs
Standing, so the patient can leave quickly afterward
Seated on a tall backless stool
Perched on the edge of an exam table without support

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A patient with a fainting history should be in a chair with armrests or supine so that, if syncope occurs, they are already supported and cannot fall and be injured. Why the others are wrong: **B** drawing a blood specimen on a standing patient is unsafe and risks a fall; **C** a backless stool offers no support if the patient loses consciousness; **D** an unsupported edge of a table provides no fall protection.

questions.stem: A phlebotomist receives a requisition that is missing the ordering provider's name. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Discard the requisition and ignore the order
Collect the specimen and write in any provider's name
Clarify and complete the missing information with the appropriate staff before collecting the specimen
Collect the specimen and leave the provider field blank

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** An incomplete requisition must be clarified and corrected through the proper channel before collection, so the order is valid and results route correctly. Why the others are wrong: **B** inventing a provider name falsifies the record; **A** discarding a needed order delays patient care without authority; **D** leaving the field blank produces an order that cannot be properly verified or billed.

questions.stem: Which two pieces of information are acceptable patient identifiers for confirming identity before a blood draw? (Select two.)

options.text: The patient's full legal name
The patient's date of birth
The patient's room number
The phlebotomist's assigned shift

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Full name and date of birth are patient-specific identifiers used to confirm identity against the requisition and wristband. Why the others are wrong: **C** a room number is a location, not a patient identifier, because patients change rooms; **D** the phlebotomist's shift has nothing to do with verifying the patient's identity.

questions.stem: A patient sits down and rolls up a sleeve when the phlebotomist explains a blood draw has been ordered. This best illustrates which type of consent?

options.text: Consent by proxy
Written informed consent
Involuntary consent
Implied consent

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** By voluntarily presenting the arm after the procedure is explained, the patient demonstrates implied consent through cooperative action. Why the others are wrong: **B** written informed consent requires a signed document, which was not described; **C** consent is by definition voluntary, so "involuntary consent" is a contradiction; **A** proxy consent involves a legally authorized representative deciding for a patient who cannot, which is not this scenario.

questions.stem: When using an evacuated tube system for routine venipuncture, at approximately what angle should the needle be inserted into the vein?

options.text: 45 to 60 degrees relative to the arm
15 to 30 degrees relative to the arm
90 degrees, straight down into the arm
Less than 5 degrees, nearly flat against the skin

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A shallow insertion angle of about 15 to 30 degrees follows the vein's path and reduces the chance of going through the back wall. Why the others are wrong: **A** 45 to 60 degrees is too steep and risks puncturing the far wall of the vein; **C** a 90-degree entry is appropriate only for certain other injections, not antecubital venipuncture; **D** an almost-flat angle under 5 degrees often fails to enter the vein lumen.

questions.stem: Which vein is generally the first choice for routine venipuncture in the antecubital fossa because of its size and relatively low risk?

options.text: Median cubital vein
Basilic vein
Cephalic vein
Brachial artery

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The median cubital vein is typically large, well anchored, and located away from major nerves and arteries, making it the preferred first choice. Why the others are wrong: **B** the basilic vein is a last choice because it lies near the brachial artery and median nerve; **C** the cephalic vein is acceptable but often harder to anchor and a second choice; **D** the brachial artery is an artery, not a venipuncture target.

questions.stem: A tourniquet should not remain applied longer than which time limit during a routine venipuncture?

options.text: There is no time limit
Five minutes
Ten minutes
One minute

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A tourniquet should be left on no longer than one minute to avoid hemoconcentration that alters analytes such as proteins and potassium. Why the others are wrong: **B** five minutes greatly exceeds the limit and causes hemoconcentration; **C** ten minutes is far too long and will distort results and patient comfort; **A** there is in fact a one-minute guideline, so claiming none exists is incorrect.

questions.stem: Which antiseptic is routinely used to cleanse the skin before a standard venipuncture?

options.text: Sterile water
70% isopropyl alcohol
Hydrogen peroxide
Povidone-iodine, which is required for every routine draw

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** 70% isopropyl alcohol is the standard antiseptic for routine venipuncture; it is applied in a circular or back-and-forth motion and allowed to air dry. Why the others are wrong: **A** sterile water does not disinfect the skin; **C** hydrogen peroxide is not the standard venipuncture antiseptic; **D** povidone-iodine is reserved for special cases like blood cultures, not required for every routine draw.

questions.stem: Immediately after filling an additive tube such as a lavender-top, what must the phlebotomist do to maintain specimen integrity?

options.text: Centrifuge the tube before any mixing
Shake the tube vigorously to dissolve the additive quickly
Gently invert the tube several times to mix the blood with the additive
Leave the tube completely still so cells settle

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Additive tubes must be gently inverted the manufacturer's recommended number of times so the anticoagulant or clot activator mixes evenly and the specimen stays usable. Why the others are wrong: **B** vigorous shaking causes hemolysis, which can ruin the specimen; **A** centrifuging before mixing does not properly distribute the additive and an EDTA tube should not be spun for a CBC; **D** leaving an anticoagulant tube unmixed allows clots to form, invalidating the sample.

questions.stem: A coagulation specimen is collected in a light-blue (sodium citrate) tube. Why is it important that this tube is filled to its indicated fill line?

options.text: An incorrect blood-to-anticoagulant ratio will produce inaccurate coagulation results
Overfilling is harmless and improves accuracy
The citrate tube does not need a specific fill volume
The fill line only matters for tubes without additives

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Sodium citrate tubes rely on a fixed 9:1 blood-to-anticoagulant ratio, so a short draw skews the ratio and yields inaccurate PT/PTT results. Why the others are wrong: **B** overfilling also distorts the ratio and is not harmless; **C** the citrate tube specifically requires an exact fill volume; **D** fill accuracy matters most for additive tubes, the opposite of the claim.

questions.stem: Midway through a venipuncture, the area around the needle begins to swell and a bruise forms. What is the most likely complication, and what should the phlebotomist do?

options.text: Hemolysis is occurring; continue and label the specimen as hemolyzed
A hematoma is forming; discontinue the draw, remove the needle, and apply pressure
The patient is fainting; lay them flat and continue the draw
Petechiae are appearing; tighten the tourniquet and proceed

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Localized swelling and bruising at the site indicate a hematoma from blood leaking into tissue; the phlebotomist should stop, remove the needle, and apply firm pressure. Why the others are wrong: **A** hemolysis is rupture of red cells inside the specimen, not visible arm swelling; **C** syncope involves loss of consciousness, not localized swelling, and you would not continue a draw on a fainting patient; **D** petechiae are tiny red spots, and tightening the tourniquet would worsen, not fix, the problem.

questions.stem: Which two practices increase the risk of hemolyzing a blood specimen? (Select two.)

options.text: Drawing blood forcefully through a needle that is too small for the vein
Vigorously shaking the tube after collection
Allowing the alcohol to air dry before puncture
Filling tubes in the correct order of draw

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Forcing blood through a too-small needle and vigorously shaking the tube both shear red blood cells, causing hemolysis that falsely elevates analytes such as potassium. Why the others are wrong: **C** letting alcohol air dry prevents stinging and contamination, reducing problems rather than causing hemolysis; **D** correct order of draw prevents additive carryover, not hemolysis.

questions.stem: When performing a dermal (capillary) puncture on an adult fingerstick, which finger and site are most appropriate?

options.text: The tip of the thumb
The center of the fingertip pad, straight down
The side of the fingertip of the middle or ring finger, slightly off-center
The fifth (little) finger because it has the most tissue

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The recommended site is the fleshy side, slightly off-center, of the middle or ring finger, where tissue is thick enough and away from bone. Why the others are wrong: **B** the very center of the pad is more painful and has more nerve endings; **A** the thumb has a pulse and calluses and is avoided; **D** the little finger has too little tissue, risking bone injury.

questions.stem: Which two practices help ensure a quality specimen during a dermal (capillary) collection? (Select two.)

options.text: Wipe away the first drop of blood before collecting
Allow blood to flow freely rather than strongly milking the site
Vigorously squeeze (milk) the finger to speed up flow
Collect the very first drop because it is the most concentrated

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Wiping away the first drop removes excess tissue fluid and alcohol residue, and letting blood flow freely (rather than forcefully milking) avoids diluting the sample with interstitial fluid and causing hemolysis. Why the others are wrong: **C** strongly milking the site introduces tissue fluid and hemolyzes the specimen; **D** the first drop is contaminated with tissue fluid and is discarded, not collected.

questions.stem: A heelstick is ordered on a newborn. Which area of the heel is the correct site for the puncture?

options.text: The arch of the foot
The exact center of the heel for the deepest sample
The posterior curve of the heel
The medial or lateral plantar surface of the heel, avoiding the central arch and the back curve

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The safe heelstick site is the medial or lateral plantar surface, where the bone is farther from the skin, reducing the risk of bone injury. Why the others are wrong: **B** the central heel is over the calcaneus and risks osteomyelitis; **C** the posterior curve also lies too close to bone; **A** the arch contains nerves, tendons, and bone and must be avoided.

questions.stem: After a routine venipuncture, what is the correct way to achieve hemostasis at the puncture site?

options.text: Apply direct pressure to the site with gauze until bleeding stops, then apply a bandage
Have the patient bend the arm tightly at the elbow and lower it
Vigorously rub the site to disperse the blood
Apply a bandage immediately without any pressure

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Direct, steady pressure with gauze until bleeding stops, followed by a bandage, allows a clot to form and prevents hematoma. Why the others are wrong: **B** bending the arm can reopen the site and is less effective than direct pressure; **C** rubbing the site can dislodge the forming clot and cause bruising; **D** bandaging without pressure lets the site continue to bleed under the bandage.

questions.stem: Which two findings should prompt the phlebotomist to immediately stop a venipuncture? (Select two.)

options.text: The patient reports sudden severe shooting pain radiating down the arm
The site rapidly swells, suggesting a hematoma
Blood begins to flow steadily into the tube
The tube reaches its proper fill line

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Sudden radiating pain can signal nerve involvement, and rapid swelling indicates a hematoma; both require immediately stopping the draw. Why the others are wrong: **C** steady blood flow into the tube is the expected, desired sign of a successful draw; **D** reaching the proper fill line means the tube is correctly collected, not a reason to abort.

questions.stem: Place these evacuated tubes in the correct CLSI order of draw for a multi-tube venipuncture, from first to last.

options.text: Light-blue top (sodium citrate)
Gold/red SST (serum, clot activator/gel)
Green top (heparin)
Lavender top (EDTA)
Gray top (sodium fluoride/potassium oxalate)

questions.explanation: The CLSI order of draw minimizes additive carryover between tubes. After any blood-culture (sterile) tubes, the sequence is: light-blue sodium citrate first so the coagulation specimen is uncontaminated, then the gold/red serum (SST) tube, then green heparin, then lavender EDTA, and finally gray sodium fluoride/oxalate. Drawing EDTA or heparin before the citrate or serum tubes would carry potassium or anticoagulant forward and skew coagulation, chemistry, and electrolyte results, so this fixed sequence protects specimen integrity.

questions.stem: Why must the skin be cleansed with a more rigorous antiseptic (such as chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine) before collecting blood cultures?

options.text: To prevent the blood from clotting in the bottle
To speed up blood flow into the bottles
To minimize skin-flora contamination that could cause a false-positive culture
Because alcohol cannot be used near culture bottles

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Rigorous antisepsis reduces normal skin flora so that any organisms recovered reflect a true bloodstream infection rather than contamination, avoiding false positives. Why the others are wrong: **B** antiseptic choice does not affect blood flow rate; **A** preventing clotting is the role of the culture bottle's medium, not the skin prep; **D** alcohol is in fact part of the typical two-step antisepsis, so the claim is false.

questions.stem: A patient needs blood cultures plus a coagulation test and a CBC. Place these tubes/bottles in the correct CLSI order of draw, from first to last.

options.text: Blood culture bottles (sterile)
Light-blue top (sodium citrate)
Lavender top (EDTA)

questions.explanation: Blood culture bottles are always drawn first to preserve sterility and prevent contamination from non-sterile tube stoppers. The light-blue sodium citrate (coagulation) tube comes next, before any tube containing other additives, so the 9:1 ratio and clotting tests are not affected by carryover. The lavender EDTA tube for the CBC is drawn after the citrate tube because EDTA's potassium and calcium-binding additive would contaminate and invalidate a coagulation specimen if drawn first. This order protects both culture sterility and specimen integrity.

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for a 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). When is the first (baseline) specimen collected?

options.text: Whenever the patient arrives, regardless of fasting status
Thirty minutes after the patient drinks the glucose beverage
Only at the end of the 2-hour period
While the patient is fasting, before the glucose beverage is given

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The OGTT begins with a fasting baseline draw before the patient consumes the glucose load; timed specimens then follow at set intervals. Why the others are wrong: **B** a 30-minute draw is a later timed sample, not the baseline; **C** collecting only at 2 hours omits the essential fasting baseline and interval points; **A** ignoring fasting status invalidates the test's interpretation.

questions.stem: When collecting a blood specimen for blood alcohol (ethanol) testing, which antiseptic should be used to clean the site?

options.text: 70% isopropyl alcohol, as for any routine draw
A non-alcohol antiseptic such as aqueous povidone-iodine or chlorhexidine in a non-alcohol base
A tincture of iodine in alcohol
Any alcohol-based hand sanitizer applied to the site

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A non-alcohol antiseptic is required for blood alcohol collection so that the prep cannot contaminate the specimen and falsely elevate the ethanol result. Why the others are wrong: **A** isopropyl alcohol can introduce alcohol into the specimen and is contraindicated; **C** a tincture is alcohol-based and likewise risks contamination; **D** alcohol-based sanitizer on the site defeats the purpose for a legally sensitive ethanol test.

questions.stem: A newborn screening collection is performed by applying blood to a special filter-paper card. What is essential for a valid specimen?

options.text: Each printed circle is fully and evenly saturated with a single drop, without layering or smearing
Multiple small drops are layered into each circle until dark
The card is touched repeatedly to the same drop to build thickness
The circles are filled only halfway to conserve blood

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A valid newborn screen requires each circle to be completely and evenly saturated with a single large drop applied to one side, with no layering or smearing. Why the others are wrong: **B** layering multiple drops makes the spot too thick and can be rejected; **C** repeatedly touching the same drop causes uneven saturation; **D** half-filled circles provide insufficient sample and are rejected.

questions.stem: A serum separator (SST) tube is received in the lab. Before it can be centrifuged for serum, what must have occurred?

options.text: The tube must be refrigerated for 24 hours first
The tube must be centrifuged immediately while still warm from the patient
The tube must be frozen before spinning
The blood must be allowed to clot completely, typically about 30 minutes at room temperature

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Serum tubes must fully clot (about 30 minutes at room temperature) before centrifugation so the gel can separate serum cleanly from the clot. Why the others are wrong: **B** spinning before the clot forms produces fibrin strands and an incomplete separation; **C** freezing whole blood before separation lyses cells and ruins the specimen; **A** refrigerating for 24 hours before spinning is unnecessary and can affect certain analytes.

questions.stem: A specimen for bilirubin is collected. Which handling step is most important to preserve its integrity?

options.text: Keep the specimen warmed to body temperature in an incubator
Protect the specimen from light, because bilirubin breaks down with light exposure
Expose the specimen to bright light to stabilize it
Shake the specimen periodically during transport

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Bilirubin is light-sensitive and degrades when exposed to light, so the specimen must be protected from light (e.g., an amber tube or foil) to keep results accurate. Why the others are wrong: **A** bilirubin specimens are not kept warm; warming is reserved for analytes like cold agglutinins; **C** light exposure destroys bilirubin rather than stabilizing it; **D** shaking causes hemolysis, which also interferes with bilirubin measurement.

questions.stem: A specimen is collected for a chain-of-custody drug screen. Which handling requirement is unique to this forensic specimen?

options.text: Any staff member may relabel the specimen as needed
The specimen may be left unsealed for convenience during transport
A documented, signed record accounts for the specimen's possession from collection through testing
Chain-of-custody documentation is optional if the lab is trusted

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Forensic specimens require an unbroken chain-of-custody form documenting and signing for every transfer of possession, so the specimen is defensible as evidence. Why the others are wrong: **B** the specimen must be sealed with tamper-evident measures, not left open; **A** uncontrolled relabeling breaks the chain and invalidates the specimen; **D** the documentation is mandatory for legal admissibility, never optional.

questions.stem: The laboratory information system flags a potassium result as a critical (panic) value. Which two actions are required immediately? (Select two.)

options.text: Notify the responsible caregiver without delay
Document the notification, including a read-back, per protocol
File the result in the chart for the provider to find later
Disregard it because instruments sometimes flag values

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A critical value signals a potentially life-threatening condition, so it must be reported to the responsible caregiver without delay and the call documented with a read-back to confirm accuracy. Why the others are wrong: **C** simply filing it for later defeats the urgent purpose of a critical-value alert; **D** ignoring a flagged critical value risks serious patient harm.

questions.stem: A whole-blood specimen must be transported to a reference lab that requires it kept chilled. Which method is appropriate?

options.text: Place the specimen in crushed ice or an ice-water slurry so it cools evenly
Place the specimen directly on a single large ice cube
Put the specimen in a freezer to chill it faster
Leave the specimen at room temperature since chilling is optional

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Chilled specimens should be placed in crushed ice or an ice-water slurry, which surrounds the tube and cools it evenly without freezing. Why the others are wrong: **B** a single large cube cools unevenly and may freeze one spot while leaving the rest warm; **C** freezing a whole-blood specimen lyses cells and is not the same as chilling; **D** ignoring a chilling requirement allows temperature-sensitive analytes to degrade.

questions.stem: A phlebotomist is assigned to draw a patient who is on airborne precautions for active pulmonary tuberculosis. Which respiratory protection is required before entering the room?

options.text: A standard surgical mask
No respiratory protection if the patient is wearing a mask
A face shield alone
A fit-tested N95 (or higher) respirator

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Airborne precautions for tuberculosis require a fit-tested N95 or higher-level respirator because the organism travels on tiny droplet nuclei that a surgical mask cannot filter. Why the others are wrong: **A** a surgical mask blocks larger droplets but not airborne nuclei; **C** a face shield protects against splashes, not inhaled particles; **B** the worker still needs respiratory protection even if the patient is masked, because aerosols persist in the room.

questions.stem: When removing (doffing) contaminated personal protective equipment after a blood draw in an isolation room, which item is generally removed first?

options.text: Gloves
Respirator or mask
Gown only after leaving the room
Eye protection before anything else

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Gloves are considered the most contaminated item and are removed first so the hands do not transfer pathogens while taking off the remaining PPE. Why the others are wrong: **B** the mask or respirator is removed last, after leaving the room, by its straps; **C** the gown is removed before exiting, not after; **D** eye protection is removed after gloves and hand hygiene, not first.

questions.stem: A sharps container at a draw station is filled to the top with used needles. What is the correct action?

options.text: Press the contents down to make room for more sharps
Empty the container into the regular trash and reuse it
Replace it once it reaches the fill line (about three-quarters full) and never overfill it
Leave it in place until the end of the month

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A sharps container must be closed and replaced when it reaches the manufacturer's fill line, typically about three-quarters full, to prevent injuries from protruding sharps. Why the others are wrong: **A** pushing the contents down exposes the worker to needlestick injury; **B** sharps are regulated medical waste and can never go in regular trash, nor can the container be reused; **D** an overfilled container is a hazard and cannot be left until an arbitrary date.

questions.stem: The hepatitis B vaccination series is offered to phlebotomists under OSHA rules. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The employer must offer the vaccine at no cost, and the employee may decline by signing a declination form
The employee must pay for the vaccine before starting work
The vaccine is mandatory and cannot be declined under any circumstances
The vaccine is only offered after a documented exposure occurs

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** OSHA requires the employer to offer the hepatitis B vaccine at no cost to at-risk workers, and an employee who declines must sign a declination statement. Why the others are wrong: **B** the cost cannot be passed to the employee; **C** the worker may decline, so it is not absolutely mandatory; **D** the vaccine is offered before exposure as a preventive measure, not only afterward.

questions.stem: A phlebotomist needs to clean visibly soiled hands after removing gloves following a draw. Which method is required in this situation?

options.text: Alcohol-based hand rub, because it is faster than soap
Washing with soap and running water
Wiping the hands on a clean towel
Applying a fresh pair of gloves over the soiled hands

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** When hands are visibly soiled, they must be washed with soap and running water, because alcohol rubs do not remove visible dirt or organic material. Why the others are wrong: **A** an alcohol rub is appropriate only when hands are not visibly soiled; **C** wiping on a towel does not decontaminate; **D** gloving over dirty hands traps contamination and does not clean them.

questions.stem: A small fire ignites in a supply area of the laboratory. According to the RACE acronym for fire response, what does the first letter direct staff to do?

options.text: Activate the alarm immediately
Rescue or remove anyone in immediate danger
Confine the fire by closing doors
Extinguish the fire with any available water

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** In the RACE response, R stands for Rescue, directing staff first to remove or rescue anyone in immediate danger from the fire. Why the others are wrong: **A** activating the Alarm is the second step (A); **C** Confining the fire by closing doors is the third step (C); **D** Extinguishing is the final step (E) and only for small, contained fires with the correct extinguisher.

questions.stem: Which two organisms are bloodborne pathogens of primary concern addressed by OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard? (Select two.)

options.text: Hepatitis C virus (HCV)
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Influenza virus

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Hepatitis C and HIV are classic bloodborne pathogens transmitted through contact with infected blood, central to OSHA's standard (along with hepatitis B). Why the others are wrong: **C** tuberculosis is spread by the airborne route, not primarily through blood; **D** influenza is spread by respiratory droplets, not bloodborne exposure.

questions.stem: A new lot of glucose meter test strips arrives and the control results fall outside the acceptable range printed for that lot. What should the phlebotomist do?

options.text: Run patient samples anyway and note the control issue afterward
Discard the control documentation and rerun only patients
Adjust the patient results upward to compensate
Stop testing patients on that meter, troubleshoot, and do not report results until controls are in range

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Out-of-range controls mean the system is not reliable, so patient testing must stop and the problem be resolved before any results are reported. Why the others are wrong: **A** reporting patient results when QC has failed risks inaccurate, unsafe results; **C** manually adjusting results fabricates data and is never acceptable; **B** discarding QC records violates documentation requirements and hides a real problem.

questions.stem: A visitor in the waiting room asks a phlebotomist whether a specific named patient is currently being seen in the lab. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Confirm the patient is there so the visitor can wait
Neither confirm nor deny the patient's presence, citing privacy policy
Provide the patient's room or station number
Ask the patient's diagnosis before deciding what to share

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under HIPAA, even confirming that a named individual is a patient is protected information, so the phlebotomist should not confirm or deny presence without authorization. Why the others are wrong: **A** confirming presence discloses PHI; **C** revealing a location compounds the disclosure; **D** the diagnosis is irrelevant and asking about it is itself an inappropriate handling of PHI.

questions.stem: Which document is the primary source of information about the hazards, safe handling, and spill response for a chemical reagent used in the laboratory?

options.text: The Safety Data Sheet (SDS) for that chemical
The patient's requisition form
The laboratory's QC log
The biohazard waste manifest

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Safety Data Sheet provides standardized information on a chemical's hazards, PPE, storage, and spill/first-aid procedures, as required by OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard. Why the others are wrong: **B** a requisition concerns the test order, not chemical hazards; **C** a QC log tracks instrument performance, not chemical safety; **D** a waste manifest documents disposal of biohazard waste, not reagent handling.

questions.stem: A phlebotomist must draw blood from a 4-year-old who is frightened and crying. Which approach best supports communication and cooperation?

options.text: Tell the child the procedure will not hurt at all
Speak calmly, be honest that there will be a quick pinch, and involve the caregiver for comfort
Proceed quickly without speaking to avoid prolonging distress
Threaten that the child will get a longer needle if they do not hold still

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Calm, honest, age-appropriate communication paired with caregiver support builds trust and cooperation with a pediatric patient. Why the others are wrong: **A** falsely promising no pain destroys trust when the child feels the stick; **C** ignoring the child increases fear and is poor practice; **D** threatening a child is unethical and counterproductive.

questions.stem: A phlebotomist enters a room to draw a sleeping inpatient. What is the correct first step?

options.text: Draw the blood quietly without waking the patient to avoid distress
Confirm identity with the patient in the next bed
Match only the wristband while the patient sleeps
Gently wake the patient and actively verify identity before proceeding

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The patient must be awakened and asked to actively state identifiers so identity can be confirmed against the wristband and requisition before any draw. Why the others are wrong: **A** drawing without verifying identity risks a wrong-patient error; **C** relying on the wristband alone omits the patient's active confirmation; **B** the neighboring patient cannot verify this patient's identity.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old arrives alone requesting a blood draw ordered by a clinic. For most routine medical testing of a minor, who generally must provide consent?

options.text: The minor alone, regardless of the test
A parent or legal guardian, unless a recognized exception applies
The phlebotomist on the minor's behalf
Any adult who accompanies the minor

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Minors generally cannot consent to their own medical care, so a parent or legal guardian must consent unless a recognized exception (such as emancipation or specific confidential services) applies. Why the others are wrong: **A** a minor cannot ordinarily give independent consent for routine testing; **C** the phlebotomist has no authority to consent for the patient; **D** an unrelated accompanying adult is not a legal guardian.

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for a lipid panel. Which instruction is typically given regarding preparation?

options.text: Eat a large meal one hour before the draw
Exercise vigorously just before the draw
Drink no fluids at all for 24 hours
Fast (water only) for the period specified by the provider, commonly 9 to 12 hours

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A fasting lipid panel commonly requires the patient to consume nothing but water for a provider-specified period, often 9 to 12 hours, so triglyceride and related results are accurate. Why the others are wrong: **A** eating before the draw defeats the fast and skews results; **C** withholding all fluids risks dehydration and is not the instruction—water is allowed; **B** vigorous exercise can affect certain analytes and is not part of standard lipid prep.

questions.stem: A basal state specimen is requested. Under what condition is a true basal-state sample collected?

options.text: In the early morning after the patient has fasted and rested overnight, before activity
Immediately after the patient climbs a flight of stairs
In the late afternoon following lunch
Right after the patient drinks a sugary beverage

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The basal state exists in the early morning, about 12 hours after the last meal, when the patient has rested and not yet been active, giving the most stable baseline. Why the others are wrong: **B** physical activity such as stair climbing alters analytes and breaks the basal state; **C** an afternoon post-lunch draw is neither fasting nor at rest; **D** a sugary drink directly raises glucose, the opposite of basal conditions.

questions.stem: A phlebotomist reviews a requisition and finds the test ordered does not match the diagnosis code, raising doubt about what was intended. What is the best action?

options.text: Choose whichever test seems more clinically likely and draw for it
Contact the ordering provider or appropriate staff to clarify before collecting
Draw extra tubes to cover both possibilities and let the lab decide
Cancel the order without telling anyone

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A discrepancy on the requisition must be clarified with the provider or appropriate staff before collection so the correct test is drawn. Why the others are wrong: **A** guessing the intended test risks the wrong collection and patient impact; **C** drawing extra tubes without an order wastes specimen and does not resolve the ambiguity; **D** silently canceling an order delays care and exceeds the phlebotomist's authority.

questions.stem: Which two communication behaviors best demonstrate professionalism and help build patient trust before a venipuncture? (Select two.)

options.text: Introducing yourself and explaining what you are going to do
Making eye contact and listening to the patient's concerns
Discussing another patient's results to seem knowledgeable
Rushing the patient so the schedule stays on time

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Introducing yourself with an explanation and using attentive eye contact and listening establish rapport and trust with the patient. Why the others are wrong: **C** discussing another patient's results breaches confidentiality and is unprofessional; **D** rushing the patient undermines trust and can increase anxiety and errors.

questions.stem: For a routine seated outpatient venipuncture, how should the patient's arm be positioned?

options.text: Bent sharply upward at the elbow
Extended downward in a straight line from shoulder to wrist, well supported
Raised above the level of the heart
Hanging freely off the side of the chair without support

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The arm should be extended in a straight, slightly downward line from shoulder to wrist and well supported so the veins are accessible and the limb is stable. Why the others are wrong: **A** a sharply bent elbow makes the antecubital veins harder to access; **C** raising the arm above the heart reduces venous filling; **D** an unsupported arm can move during the draw and risks injury.

questions.stem: Which needle gauge has the smallest bore (narrowest lumen)?

options.text: 21 gauge
16 gauge
18 gauge
23 gauge

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Needle gauge is inversely related to bore size, so the highest number, 23 gauge, has the smallest (narrowest) lumen. Why the others are wrong: **A** 21 gauge is wider than 23 gauge; **C** 18 gauge is wider still; **B** 16 gauge has one of the largest bores listed, the opposite of smallest.

questions.stem: A phlebotomist is collecting blood from a hand vein on a patient with fragile veins. Which device is most appropriate for this site?

options.text: A winged infusion (butterfly) set with a small-gauge needle
A large 16-gauge straight needle
A syringe with an 18-gauge needle drawn rapidly
A lancet used as for a fingerstick

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A winged (butterfly) set with a small-gauge needle gives better control on small or fragile hand veins and a shallow angle, reducing the chance of going through the vein. Why the others are wrong: **B** a 16-gauge needle is far too large for a fragile hand vein and would damage it; **C** a rapid 18-gauge syringe draw risks collapsing the vein and hemolysis; **D** a lancet is for capillary dermal puncture, not venipuncture of a hand vein.

questions.stem: While palpating to locate a vein, the phlebotomist feels a strong pulse beneath the fingertip. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: A well-anchored vein ideal for puncture
An artery, which should not be used for routine venipuncture
A tendon that will roll away
A sclerosed vein that is safe to use

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A pulse indicates an artery; routine venipuncture targets veins, so a pulsating vessel must be avoided to prevent arterial puncture. Why the others are wrong: **A** veins do not pulse, so a pulse does not signal a good vein; **C** a tendon feels firm and cord-like but does not pulse; **D** a sclerosed (hardened) vein feels hard and is also unsuitable, but it does not produce a pulse.

questions.stem: How far above the intended venipuncture site should the tourniquet typically be applied?

options.text: Directly over the puncture site
On the wrist, below the site
About 3 to 4 inches above the site
Around the upper chest

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The tourniquet is applied about 3 to 4 inches proximal to (above) the intended site so it engorges the veins without obscuring the puncture area. Why the others are wrong: **A** placing it over the site would obstruct the puncture; **B** a tourniquet below the site does not impede venous return at the draw location; **D** the chest is anatomically inappropriate and ineffective for an arm draw.

questions.stem: After a clean venipuncture entry, blood stops flowing into the tube even though the needle appears to be in the vein. What is a reasonable first adjustment?

options.text: Immediately withdraw the needle and start over in the other arm
Probe blindly and laterally to find more blood
Slightly rotate the bevel or gently adjust needle depth, as the bevel may be against the vein wall
Tighten the tourniquet to a painful degree

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** When flow stops, the bevel may be resting against the vein wall, so a slight rotation of the bevel or minor depth adjustment often restores flow. Why the others are wrong: **A** abandoning the draw immediately is premature when a small adjustment may work; **B** blind lateral probing can cause nerve injury and hematoma and is not acceptable; **D** painfully overtightening the tourniquet harms the patient and does not address bevel position.

questions.stem: During a draw, the patient suddenly becomes pale, sweaty, and says they feel faint. What should the phlebotomist do first?

options.text: Continue and finish the draw quickly before the patient passes out
Remove the tourniquet and needle, then support the patient and lower the head as needed
Leave the patient alone to recover
Give the patient food immediately

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** At the first signs of syncope, the phlebotomist must discontinue the draw by removing the tourniquet and needle, then protect the patient and lower the head to improve cerebral perfusion. Why the others are wrong: **A** continuing risks the patient losing consciousness with a needle in the arm; **C** leaving the patient alone is unsafe during impending syncope; **D** giving food to a near-fainting patient risks aspiration and is not the immediate priority.

questions.stem: A multi-tube draw includes a tube for trace-element (e.g., zinc) testing in a royal-blue top. Where does specialized trace-element handling place this tube relative to additive carryover concerns?

options.text: Trace-element tubes are designed to avoid contamination from tube materials, and a dedicated/first draw is used to prevent trace-metal carryover
Trace-element tubes may be filled last after EDTA without concern
Trace-element testing has no special tube requirements
Any glass tube is acceptable for trace elements

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Royal-blue trace-element tubes are specially manufactured to be low in trace metals, and they are handled to avoid carryover so the trace-metal result is not contaminated. Why the others are wrong: **B** drawing after EDTA risks additive and metal carryover that can skew trace results; **C** trace-element testing has stringent tube requirements, not none; **D** ordinary glass tubes can leach trace metals and are not acceptable.

questions.stem: Which capillary collection device is designed to fill by capillary action and contains a small amount of anticoagulant for certain tests?

options.text: A microcollection (microtainer) tube
A large evacuated 10 mL tube
A blood culture bottle
A urine specimen cup

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Microcollection tubes (microtainers) are small devices that fill by capillary action and come with color-coded additives appropriate to the test, ideal for the tiny volumes of a dermal puncture. Why the others are wrong: **B** a 10 mL evacuated tube is for venous draws and far exceeds capillary volumes; **C** a blood culture bottle is for venous blood cultures, not capillary collection; **D** a urine cup is unrelated to blood collection.

questions.stem: When performing a fingerstick that will fill multiple microcollection tubes, which is collected first to minimize platelet clumping and clotting effects?

options.text: Serum (clot) microtube first
The EDTA (hematology) microtube first, then other additives, then serum last
Gray-top microtube first
Order does not matter for capillary collection

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** For capillary (dermal) collection, the order of draw is reversed from venipuncture: EDTA hematology tubes are filled first to get an accurate cell count before platelets begin clumping, with serum tubes last. Why the others are wrong: **A** filling serum first delays the EDTA count and risks platelet clumping in the hematology sample; **C** the gray top is not collected before the EDTA hematology tube in capillary order; **D** order does matter in capillary collection to protect the cell count.

questions.stem: A patient calls out that they feel a sharp, electric, shooting sensation down the forearm the moment the needle is inserted. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Continue the draw because the sensation will pass
Push the needle deeper to relieve the sensation
Remove the needle promptly, as this may indicate nerve involvement
Rotate the arm forcefully while leaving the needle in

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A sharp, electric, radiating sensation suggests the needle has contacted or irritated a nerve, so the needle should be removed promptly to prevent injury. Why the others are wrong: **A** continuing risks lasting nerve damage; **B** advancing the needle deeper would worsen potential nerve injury; **D** forcefully rotating the arm with the needle in place could cause further trauma.

questions.stem: Which two practices help preserve specimen integrity between collection and testing? (Select two.)

options.text: Deliver specimens to the lab within the required time window
Store specimens at the temperature specified for each test
Leave specimens on a sunny windowsill until pickup
Repeatedly warm and rechill a specimen during transport

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Timely delivery and storing each specimen at its required temperature keep analytes stable so results stay accurate. Why the others are wrong: **C** sunlight raises temperature and degrades light-sensitive analytes such as bilirubin; **D** cycling a specimen between warm and cold destabilizes analytes and can damage cells.

questions.stem: Place the following core steps of a routine evacuated-tube venipuncture in the correct sequence, from first to last (assume the patient is identified and supplies are ready).

options.text: Apply the tourniquet and select the vein
Cleanse the site with antiseptic and let it air dry
Insert the needle and collect tubes in order of draw
Remove the needle, activate the safety device, and apply pressure

questions.explanation: The correct sequence is to first apply the tourniquet and select/palpate the vein, then cleanse the site with antiseptic and allow it to air dry so it does not sting or contaminate the puncture, then insert the needle and collect the tubes in the proper order of draw, and finally remove the needle, engage its safety device, and apply pressure to the site. Cleansing must precede puncture, collection must precede needle removal, and safe needle disposal with hemostasis closes the procedure. Performing these out of order risks contamination, an unsafe stick, or a needlestick injury.

questions.stem: Two sets of blood cultures are ordered. Why are multiple culture sites/sets and adequate blood volume important?

options.text: They improve the chance of detecting true pathogens and help distinguish real infection from contamination
They are required only to use up extra bottles
They reduce the need for skin antisepsis
They allow the same puncture to be reused repeatedly

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Collecting adequate volume and more than one set increases the likelihood of recovering true bloodstream pathogens and helps separate genuine infection from a single contaminated set. Why the others are wrong: **B** the practice has a clinical rationale, not bottle usage; **C** rigorous antisepsis is still required for every set; **D** each set uses fresh antisepsis and technique, not a reused puncture.

questions.stem: A point-of-care hemoglobin and hematocrit (H&H) is performed at the bedside. What is the main advantage of point-of-care testing?

options.text: It eliminates the need for any quality control
It removes the need to identify the patient
It is always more accurate than the central laboratory
It provides rapid results near the patient, speeding clinical decisions

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Point-of-care testing delivers fast results at or near the patient's side, allowing quicker clinical decisions. Why the others are wrong: **A** POC devices still require quality control; **C** POC results are convenient but not inherently more accurate than the central lab; **B** patient identification is always required regardless of where testing occurs.

questions.stem: A therapeutic drug monitoring test requires a trough level. When is a trough specimen typically collected?

options.text: Immediately after the dose is administered
At the random peak of drug concentration
Just before the next scheduled dose, when the drug level is lowest
Halfway between two doses regardless of timing

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A trough level is drawn just before the next dose, when the drug concentration is at its lowest, to confirm it stays within the therapeutic range. Why the others are wrong: **A** drawing right after a dose captures a peak or rising level, not a trough; **B** the peak is a different timed sample, the opposite of a trough; **D** an arbitrary midpoint does not reliably capture the lowest concentration.

questions.stem: A 24-hour urine collection is ordered. What instruction is essential for a valid timed urine specimen?

options.text: Collect only the first morning void and discard the rest
Discard the first void to start timing, then collect all urine for 24 hours including the final void
Refrigerate nothing and leave the container open
Collect random samples whenever convenient

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A proper 24-hour collection begins by discarding the first void to mark the start time, then saving every subsequent void for 24 hours, ending with a final void at the 24-hour mark, so the timed total is accurate. Why the others are wrong: **A** collecting only one void is not a 24-hour specimen; **C** many 24-hour collections require refrigeration or a preservative, and leaving it open invites contamination; **D** random sampling does not capture the complete timed output.

questions.stem: Which two practices are appropriate when collecting a specimen for a legal (forensic) drug screen? (Select two.)

options.text: Maintain a documented chain of custody for the specimen
Verify the donor's identity and use tamper-evident seals
Allow the specimen to be unattended between steps
Let any available person sign the custody form on the collector's behalf

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Forensic drug screens require an unbroken, documented chain of custody plus verified donor identity and tamper-evident sealing so the result is legally defensible. Why the others are wrong: **C** leaving the specimen unattended breaks the chain of custody; **D** the actual collector must sign the form, not an arbitrary substitute, or the chain is invalidated.

questions.stem: After centrifuging a serum separator tube, what is the correct way to handle the tube before testing?

options.text: Recentrifuge it several more times for clarity
Leave it undisturbed with the gel barrier intact between serum and cells
Shake it to remix serum and cells
Pour the serum and cells back together

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** After spinning, the gel barrier separates serum from cells and the tube should be left undisturbed so the serum stays cleanly separated for testing. Why the others are wrong: **A** repeated recentrifugation is unnecessary and can affect some analytes; **C** shaking remixes cells into the serum and ruins the separation; **D** recombining serum and cells defeats the purpose of the separator tube.

questions.stem: To prepare an aliquot from a centrifuged serum tube, which practice protects specimen integrity and safety?

options.text: Use a clean transfer pipette, avoid disturbing the cells/gel, and label the aliquot tube with the patient identifiers
Pour serum quickly across multiple open tubes on the bench
Reuse the same pipette across different patients' specimens
Leave the aliquot tube unlabeled to save time

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Aliquoting requires a clean transfer device, careful pipetting that avoids the cells and gel, and labeling the aliquot with the patient's identifiers so the sample stays traceable and uncontaminated. Why the others are wrong: **B** pouring across open tubes risks spills, aerosols, and mix-ups; **C** reusing a pipette between patients cross-contaminates specimens; **D** an unlabeled aliquot loses patient identity and must never be used.

questions.stem: A specimen label is applied at the bedside immediately after collection. Which detail is essential on the label?

options.text: The phlebotomist's home address
The patient's name, a second identifier, and the date and time of collection
Only the test name
The patient's room number alone

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A proper label requires the patient's name plus a second identifier and the collection date and time so the specimen is uniquely and accurately tied to the patient. Why the others are wrong: **A** the phlebotomist's address is irrelevant to specimen identity; **C** the test name alone does not identify the patient; **D** a room number is a location, not an acceptable patient identifier.

questions.stem: A glucose specimen is delayed and was collected in a plain tube without a glycolysis inhibitor. What preanalytical error is most likely if it sits at room temperature?

options.text: The glucose value will be unaffected indefinitely
The glucose value will be falsely increased over time
The glucose value will be falsely decreased because blood cells continue to consume glucose
The specimen will clot faster and raise glucose

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Without a glycolysis inhibitor such as sodium fluoride, cells keep metabolizing glucose, so a delayed room-temperature specimen shows a falsely low glucose. Why the others are wrong: **B** ongoing glycolysis lowers, not raises, glucose; **A** the value does change with time, so it is not unaffected; **D** clotting speed does not raise glucose, and cellular consumption is the relevant effect.

questions.stem: Which two conditions would cause the laboratory to reject a received specimen? (Select two.)

options.text: The specimen is unlabeled or has a label that does not match the requisition
A coagulation (light-blue) tube is significantly underfilled (short draw)
The specimen was collected in the correct tube and properly mixed
The specimen arrived at the requested temperature within the stability window

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** An unlabeled or mismatched specimen cannot be safely linked to the patient, and a short-draw citrate tube has the wrong blood-to-anticoagulant ratio, so both are rejected. Why the others are wrong: **C** a correctly collected and mixed specimen meets acceptance criteria; **D** arriving at the proper temperature within its stability window is exactly what is required for acceptance.

questions.stem: A phlebotomist is splashed in the eyes with blood while transferring a specimen. After flushing copiously at the eyewash station, for approximately how long should irrigation continue?

options.text: About 15 minutes of continuous flushing
About 10 seconds, then dry the eyes
Until the eyes feel cool, usually under a minute
Flushing is unnecessary if vision is unaffected

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A mucous-membrane (eye) splash exposure should be flushed at an eyewash station for about 15 minutes of continuous irrigation before reporting for post-exposure evaluation. Why the others are wrong: **B** ten seconds is far too brief to dilute and remove infectious material; **C** stopping when the eyes feel cool leaves contaminant behind; **D** any blood splash to mucous membranes is an exposure that requires flushing and reporting regardless of symptoms.

questions.stem: On the NFPA 704 hazard diamond posted on a reagent storage cabinet, what does the red (top) quadrant indicate?

options.text: Health hazard
Flammability hazard
Instability/reactivity hazard
Special precautions only

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** On the NFPA 704 diamond the red top quadrant rates flammability, with higher numbers meaning a greater fire hazard. Why the others are wrong: **A** the health hazard is the blue quadrant on the left; **C** instability/reactivity is the yellow quadrant on the right; **D** special hazards (such as oxidizers or water-reactive agents) appear in the white bottom quadrant, not the red one.

questions.stem: A patient is on droplet precautions for influenza. What is the minimum personal protective equipment a phlebotomist needs to draw blood at the bedside?

options.text: A fit-tested N95 respirator and a gown
A gown and gloves only, with no facial protection
No additional PPE beyond hand hygiene
A surgical mask, plus gloves and eye protection per standard precautions

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Droplet precautions call for a surgical mask when working within close range of the patient, layered on top of standard-precaution gloves and eye protection. Why the others are wrong: **A** an N95 is reserved for airborne precautions, not droplet; **B** omitting a mask leaves the mucous membranes unprotected from respiratory droplets; **C** hand hygiene alone is insufficient for a patient on droplet precautions.

questions.stem: Which container is the correct disposal site for blood-soaked gauze and used gloves that are saturated with blood?

options.text: The sharps container
The regular office wastebasket
A biohazard (regulated medical waste) bag, typically red
The recycling bin

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Items saturated with blood are regulated medical waste and belong in a labeled biohazard bag, usually red, for proper treatment and disposal. Why the others are wrong: **A** the sharps container is reserved for needles and other sharp objects, not soft waste; **B** blood-saturated waste cannot go in ordinary trash; **D** contaminated materials are never recycled.

questions.stem: Which agency is responsible for issuing and enforcing the workplace standards that require employers to protect phlebotomists from occupational bloodborne-pathogen exposure?

options.text: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
The Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI)

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** OSHA writes and enforces the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard and other workplace safety regulations that employers must follow. Why the others are wrong: **A** the CDC issues guidelines and recommendations but is not the workplace enforcement agency; **C** the FDA regulates devices, drugs, and biologics, not workplace safety; **D** CLSI publishes voluntary consensus laboratory standards and does not enforce regulations.

questions.stem: A nurse asks a phlebotomist to add an unordered test to a patient's draw "as a favor" because the patient is already there. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Add the test, since collecting one more tube is convenient
Collect the extra tube and label it without a requisition
Explain that a valid provider order is required and the test cannot be run without one
Run the test and bill it to the patient afterward

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Laboratory testing requires a valid provider order; the phlebotomist should explain that the additional test cannot be performed without one. Why the others are wrong: **A** drawing and running a test without an order is outside scope and improper; **B** collecting an unordered tube creates an unverifiable specimen; **D** billing for an unordered test is improper and may constitute fraud.

questions.stem: Engineering and work-practice controls reduce bloodborne-pathogen exposure. Which two are examples of engineering controls? (Select two.)

options.text: Self-sheathing (safety-engineered) needles
Puncture-resistant sharps containers
A written policy telling staff not to recap needles
Reminding employees to wash their hands

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Engineering controls are physical devices that isolate or remove the hazard, such as safety-engineered needles and puncture-resistant sharps containers. Why the others are wrong: **C** a no-recapping policy changes how a task is performed, making it a work-practice control; **D** reminding staff to wash hands is also a work-practice control, not a physical engineering device.

questions.stem: A CLIA-waived urine pregnancy test is performed at a clinic. What does the CLIA "waived" classification of a test primarily indicate?

options.text: The test is simple and carries a low risk of an erroneous result when performed per instructions
The test requires no quality control of any kind
The test may only be performed by a pathologist
The facility is exempt from any CLIA oversight

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** CLIA-waived tests are simple, low-complexity procedures with a low risk of erroneous results when the manufacturer's instructions are followed. Why the others are wrong: **B** waived tests still require following QC and manufacturer instructions; **C** waived tests are designed to be performed by trained non-laboratorians, not restricted to pathologists; **D** the facility must still hold a CLIA Certificate of Waiver and follow its terms, so it is not exempt from oversight.

questions.stem: Which behavior best protects patient confidentiality when a phlebotomist discusses cases during the workday?

options.text: Reviewing patient details with a coworker in a crowded elevator
Limiting discussion of a patient's information to private areas and to staff who need to know
Leaving printed requisitions face-up at the public reception desk
Mentioning a patient's results to their friend who is in the waiting room

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Discussing patient information only in private and only with staff who have a legitimate need to know upholds HIPAA's minimum-necessary principle and protects confidentiality. Why the others are wrong: **A** talking about patients in a crowded elevator risks being overheard by unauthorized people; **C** leaving requisitions exposed at a public desk discloses PHI to passersby; **D** sharing results with a friend has no treatment purpose and is a clear breach.

questions.stem: Before using a new bottle of skin antiseptic, a phlebotomist notices the bottle is past its printed expiration date. What is the correct action?

options.text: Use it anyway because antiseptics rarely change
Use half the normal amount to compensate
Remove the expired product from use and obtain in-date antiseptic
Cross out the date and continue using the bottle

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Expired antiseptics may have reduced effectiveness, so the product should be removed from use and replaced with an in-date supply as part of routine quality control. Why the others are wrong: **A** assuming an expired antiseptic still works can compromise skin asepsis; **B** changing the amount does not restore an expired product's potency; **D** altering the expiration label is falsification and does not make the product safe.
