questions.stem: An inpatient's wristband is faded and partly illegible, and the bed label does not clearly match the requisition. What should the phlebotomist do before drawing?

options.text: Draw based on the bed label since the patient is in the assigned bed
Have the wristband verified and corrected/replaced by the nurse before collecting
Write a new band by hand and proceed
Ask the patient to confirm the bed number instead

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An unreadable or mismatched wristband must be verified and replaced by the responsible nurse so identity can be confirmed before any specimen is collected. Why the others are wrong: **A** a bed label is a location, not a reliable patient identifier; **C** the phlebotomist hand-writing a band bypasses proper identity verification; **D** a bed number is not an acceptable patient identifier.

questions.stem: In an outpatient setting where patients have no wristband, how should the phlebotomist confirm identity before a draw?

options.text: Call out the patient's name in the waiting room and draw whoever stands up
Ask the patient to actively state their full name and date of birth and match a photo ID or the requisition
Use the order in which patients signed in
Rely on recognizing a returning patient from a prior visit

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Without a wristband, identity is confirmed by having the patient actively state two identifiers (full name and date of birth) and matching them to a photo ID or the requisition. Why the others are wrong: **A** calling a name and drawing whoever responds risks a wrong-patient error if someone mishears; **C** sign-in order is not a patient identifier; **D** relying on memory of a face is unreliable and not an approved identification method.

questions.stem: An adult inpatient is confused and cannot reliably state their name. What is the most appropriate way to verify identity?

options.text: Skip identification because the patient cannot participate
Accept the confused patient's uncertain answer and proceed
Identify the patient by the diagnosis written on the chart
Use the patient's wristband identifiers and have a caregiver (e.g., nurse) confirm identity per facility policy

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** When a patient cannot actively confirm identity, the wristband identifiers are used and a caregiver such as the nurse confirms identity according to facility policy. Why the others are wrong: **A** skipping identification entirely risks a serious wrong-patient error; **B** accepting an unreliable answer from a confused patient does not establish identity; **C** a diagnosis is not a patient identifier.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for a fasting test mentions they drank black coffee and smoked a cigarette this morning. How should the phlebotomist regard the fasting status?

options.text: Black coffee and smoking do not break a fast, so no action is needed
Coffee and smoking can affect certain analytes, so the phlebotomist should note this and verify the order with the nurse or provider
Only solid food matters; report the specimen as a clean fasting sample
Reschedule the patient without consulting anyone

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A true fast generally excludes coffee and smoking because both can alter certain analytes, so the phlebotomist should document this and verify how to proceed with the nurse or provider. Why the others are wrong: **A** and **C** wrongly assume coffee and smoking are harmless to a fast, which can compromise interpretation; **D** unilaterally rescheduling without consulting the provider exceeds the phlebotomist's authority.

questions.stem: A patient declines to give their date of birth, saying it is private. What is the best professional response?

options.text: Skip the second identifier and proceed with the name only
Explain that verifying two identifiers is a safety step to ensure the right patient receives the right test
Tell the patient they cannot be tested and dismiss them
Guess the date of birth from the chart and continue

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Calmly explaining that two-identifier verification is a patient-safety measure usually gains cooperation while respecting the patient. Why the others are wrong: **A** proceeding with only one identifier fails the safety standard and risks a wrong-patient error; **C** abruptly dismissing the patient is poor communication and does not resolve the situation; **D** guessing the identifier from the chart defeats the purpose of active verification.

questions.stem: A patient has IV lines and recent draw sites in both arms, and the legs are not an option for a phlebotomist. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Draw above one of the running IVs to save time
Consult the patient's nurse or provider to determine an acceptable site or procedure
Cancel the order permanently
Reuse an old puncture site that has not fully healed

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** When standard arm sites are compromised, the phlebotomist consults the nurse or provider to identify an acceptable site or alternative procedure within policy. Why the others are wrong: **A** drawing above a running IV contaminates the specimen with IV fluid; **C** permanently canceling a needed order exceeds the phlebotomist's authority; **D** puncturing an unhealed site risks infection and poor specimen quality.

questions.stem: Which two elements should a phlebotomist confirm on a test requisition before collecting a specimen? (Select two.)

options.text: The patient's identifying information matches the patient
The specific tests ordered and any special collection requirements
The phlebotomist's personal break schedule
The brand of furniture in the draw room

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Before collection the phlebotomist confirms that the requisition's patient information matches the patient and reviews exactly which tests are ordered along with any special requirements (such as fasting or timing). Why the others are wrong: **C** the phlebotomist's break schedule has nothing to do with verifying an order; **D** the room furnishings are irrelevant to requisition review.

questions.stem: A patient who uses a wheelchair arrives for an outpatient draw. What is the best practice for positioning?

options.text: Insist the patient transfer to the draw chair even if unsafe
Draw the patient safely in the wheelchair, lock the wheels, and support the arm
Have the patient stand and lean on the counter
Refuse to draw a patient who cannot use the standard chair

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A patient can be drawn safely while seated in the wheelchair with the wheels locked and the arm well supported, avoiding an unnecessary or unsafe transfer. Why the others are wrong: **A** forcing an unsafe transfer risks a fall and injury; **C** having the patient stand risks a fall if syncope occurs; **D** refusing to accommodate the patient is inappropriate and discriminatory.

questions.stem: When should the specimen tubes be labeled during a routine venipuncture?

options.text: Immediately after collection, in the presence of the patient, before leaving the bedside
Before the draw, so the tubes are ready
Later at the workstation once several patients are done
Only if the lab requests a label

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Tubes are labeled immediately after collection, in front of the patient and before leaving, so the specimen is correctly and verifiably tied to that patient. Why the others are wrong: **B** pre-labeling empty tubes risks placing a label on a tube used for a different patient; **C** labeling later at the workstation invites mix-ups among multiple patients' tubes; **D** labeling is always required, not optional.

questions.stem: A vein cannot be felt easily and the phlebotomist wants to encourage it to become more prominent. Which technique is appropriate?

options.text: Have the patient vigorously pump the fist repeatedly
Apply a warm compress to the site to promote dilation
Slap the antecubital area sharply several times
Leave the tourniquet on for five minutes to maximize filling

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Applying a warm compress dilates the vessels and makes a vein easier to palpate without harming the specimen. Why the others are wrong: **A** vigorous fist pumping causes hemoconcentration and can falsely raise potassium; **C** slapping the site is painful, ineffective, and can cause bruising; **D** leaving the tourniquet on five minutes causes hemoconcentration and exceeds the one-minute limit.

questions.stem: In which direction should the needle bevel face during a venipuncture?

options.text: Bevel down toward the skin
Bevel up, facing away from the skin
Bevel turned sideways
Bevel direction does not matter

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The needle is inserted bevel up so the sharp opening enters the vein cleanly and blood flows freely into the system. Why the others are wrong: **A** a bevel-down entry can dig into the lower vein wall and impede flow; **C** a sideways bevel does not present the cutting edge correctly; **D** bevel orientation does matter for a clean, comfortable entry and good flow.

questions.stem: A phlebotomist suspects an accidental arterial puncture during a draw. Which finding most strongly supports this?

options.text: Bright red blood that pulses or rapidly fills the tube under noticeable pressure
Slow, dark venous blood trickling into the tube
No blood return at all
Clear straw-colored fluid entering the tube

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Bright red blood that pulses or fills the tube rapidly under pressure suggests an arterial puncture; the phlebotomist should remove the needle and apply firm, prolonged pressure. Why the others are wrong: **B** slow, dark blood is the expected appearance of normal venous blood; **C** no blood return indicates a missed vein, not an artery; **D** straw-colored fluid suggests serum or interstitial fluid, not arterial blood.

questions.stem: A patient reports a strong allergy to adhesive bandages. After bleeding has stopped, what is the best way to cover the site?

options.text: Apply the usual adhesive bandage anyway
Use gauze secured with paper tape or a self-adherent wrap the patient tolerates
Leave the site completely uncovered and open
Press a cotton ball on with the patient's own saliva

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** For an adhesive allergy, gauze held with paper tape or a self-adherent wrap that the patient tolerates protects the site without triggering a reaction. Why the others are wrong: **A** using the usual adhesive risks an allergic skin reaction; **C** leaving the site open invites contamination and continued oozing; **D** using saliva is unhygienic and inappropriate.

questions.stem: A discard (clearing) tube is recommended before a coagulation tube when a winged blood collection set is used for the draw. Why?

options.text: The air in the winged set's tubing would otherwise cause a short draw and skew the citrate ratio
It warms the needle before the real draw
It adds extra anticoagulant to the citrate tube
It is needed only for serum tubes, never coagulation tubes

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A winged set's tubing holds a small volume of air; drawing a discard tube first removes that air so the citrate tube fills completely and keeps the correct 9:1 blood-to-anticoagulant ratio. Why the others are wrong: **B** the discard tube has nothing to do with warming the needle; **C** it does not add anticoagulant; **D** the clearing tube is specifically relevant to the coagulation tube, the opposite of the claim.

questions.stem: After inserting the needle and seating the first tube, blood enters the tube. What is the correct time to release the tourniquet?

options.text: Only after all tubes are filled and the needle is removed
As soon as blood flow is established, ideally within about one minute and before removing the needle
Before the needle is even inserted
It does not need to be released at all

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The tourniquet should be released once blood flow is established, generally within one minute and before the needle is withdrawn, to limit hemoconcentration and reduce bleeding at removal. Why the others are wrong: **A** waiting until the needle is out can leave the tourniquet on too long and increase site bleeding; **C** releasing before insertion would collapse the veins you need; **D** leaving the tourniquet on indefinitely causes hemoconcentration and patient discomfort.

questions.stem: Which two veins of the antecubital area are acceptable choices for venipuncture, recognizing that one carries higher risk and is selected only when others are unavailable? (Select two.)

options.text: Median cubital vein
Cephalic vein
Brachial artery
Median nerve

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The median cubital vein is the preferred choice and the cephalic vein is an acceptable alternative; the basilic vein is reserved for when these are unavailable because it lies near the artery and nerve. Why the others are wrong: **C** the brachial artery is an artery, not a venipuncture target; **D** the median nerve is a nerve and must be avoided, not punctured.

questions.stem: A capillary specimen is needed for a newborn bilirubin level. Which handling step is specific to this dermal collection?

options.text: Protect the microcollection container from light during and after collection
Warm the heel to body temperature for 30 minutes
Collect the first drop because it is most concentrated
Vigorously squeeze the heel to fill the container faster

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Bilirubin is light-sensitive, so an amber or light-shielded microcollection container is used to keep the result accurate. Why the others are wrong: **B** brief warming aids flow, but a 30-minute warming is excessive and not the bilirubin-specific step; **C** the first drop is contaminated with tissue fluid and is wiped away, not collected; **D** vigorous squeezing introduces tissue fluid and hemolyzes the sample.

questions.stem: Two attempts at venipuncture on the same patient have failed. According to common best practice, what should the phlebotomist do next?

options.text: Keep attempting until a sample is obtained, regardless of the number of tries
Stop after two unsuccessful attempts and ask another qualified phlebotomist to try or notify the appropriate staff
Probe more aggressively on the third attempt
Switch to a fingerstick for every test regardless of requirements

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Best practice limits a phlebotomist to two attempts; after two failures, another qualified collector should try or the appropriate staff are notified, sparing the patient repeated sticks. Why the others are wrong: **A** unlimited attempts cause unnecessary pain and tissue trauma; **C** aggressive probing risks nerve injury and hematoma; **D** a fingerstick cannot satisfy tests that require a venous volume or specific tube.

questions.stem: What is the correct angle and approach for a dermal (capillary) puncture on a fingertip?

options.text: Puncture across (perpendicular to) the fingerprint grooves so the drop forms well
Puncture parallel to (along) the grooves so blood runs down them
Insert at a shallow 15-degree angle as in venipuncture
Puncture the very tip of the finger straight in

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A dermal puncture is made across (perpendicular to) the whorls of the fingerprint so blood beads into a well-rounded drop instead of running along the grooves. Why the others are wrong: **B** puncturing parallel to the grooves lets blood run down them and makes collection harder; **C** a 15-degree venipuncture angle does not apply to a perpendicular lancet puncture; **D** the very tip has little tissue and is more painful, so the fleshy side is preferred.

questions.stem: Blood cultures are drawn from two separate sites. Why are aerobic and anaerobic bottles both inoculated?

options.text: To recover organisms that grow with oxygen as well as those that grow without it
To double the patient's billing
Because one bottle is only a spare in case the other breaks
To eliminate the need for skin antisepsis

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Aerobic and anaerobic bottles support different organisms, so inoculating both maximizes recovery of aerobes and anaerobes from a possible bloodstream infection. Why the others are wrong: **B** the practice is clinical, not for billing; **C** the second bottle is not merely a spare; each cultures a different environment; **D** rigorous skin antisepsis is still required for every set.

questions.stem: A bedside point-of-care glucose is collected by fingerstick. To get a representative result, the phlebotomist should:

options.text: Use the first drop after a strong squeeze for speed
Add alcohol to the drop to thin it
Wipe away the first drop and apply a freely forming drop to the test strip
Collect blood that has been smeared across the fingertip

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Wiping away the first drop removes tissue fluid and alcohol residue, and applying a freely forming drop gives a representative glucose result. Why the others are wrong: **A** a hard squeeze adds tissue fluid and the first drop is contaminated, skewing the value; **B** alcohol added to the drop dilutes and contaminates the sample; **D** smeared blood is not a clean drop and can give an inaccurate reading.

questions.stem: A lactic acid (lactate) specimen is ordered. Which collection consideration is most important for accuracy?

options.text: Avoid prolonged tourniquet use and fist pumping, which raise lactate, and handle the specimen promptly
Leave the tourniquet on for several minutes to concentrate the sample
Have the patient exercise the arm just before the draw
Let the specimen sit at room temperature for hours before testing

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Lactate rises with stasis and muscle activity, so a lactic acid draw should minimize tourniquet time and fist pumping and be handled promptly (often chilled per protocol). Why the others are wrong: **B** prolonged tourniquet use falsely elevates lactate; **C** exercising the arm increases local lactate production; **D** delayed processing allows continued glycolysis and rising lactate.

questions.stem: Which two specimens are non-blood specimens a phlebotomist may be responsible for collecting or processing? (Select two.)

options.text: A urine sample for urinalysis
A throat swab for culture
An EDTA tube of venous blood for a CBC
A serum tube for a chemistry panel

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Urine for urinalysis and a throat swab for culture are non-blood specimens that phlebotomists may collect or process depending on facility scope. Why the others are wrong: **C** an EDTA tube of venous blood is a blood specimen; **D** a serum chemistry tube is likewise a blood specimen, not a non-blood specimen.

questions.stem: While loading a centrifuge with several specimen tubes, what must the phlebotomist do for safe, effective operation?

options.text: Balance the tubes by placing equal weights opposite each other and keep the lid closed during the spin
Place a single tube alone on one side for speed
Open the lid while it is still spinning to check progress
Remove the stoppers before spinning to release pressure

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Tubes must be balanced with equal weights placed opposite one another and the lid kept closed throughout the run for safe, effective centrifugation. Why the others are wrong: **B** a single unbalanced tube causes dangerous vibration and can break tubes; **C** opening the lid while spinning risks injury and aerosols; **D** removing stoppers before spinning can cause spills and aerosolize the specimen.

questions.stem: A separated serum aliquot must be stored before testing but cannot be analyzed for several days. Which storage method is generally appropriate to preserve most analytes long term?

options.text: Leave it at room temperature on the bench
Freeze and thaw it repeatedly to keep it mixed
Store it in direct sunlight to keep it warm
Freeze the separated serum at the temperature specified for the test

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Once serum is separated from the cells, freezing it at the temperature specified for the test preserves most analytes for longer-term storage. Why the others are wrong: **A** room-temperature storage for days degrades many analytes; **B** repeated freeze-thaw cycles damage analytes and must be avoided; **C** sunlight raises temperature and harms light-sensitive analytes.

questions.stem: When a phlebotomist logs a collected specimen into the laboratory information system (LIS), what is the main purpose of this step?

options.text: To accession and track the specimen, linking it to the patient and the ordered tests
To diagnose the patient automatically
To delete the provider's order
To replace the need for a specimen label

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Logging a specimen into the LIS accessions it, creating a tracked record that ties the sample to the correct patient and ordered tests as it moves through the lab. Why the others are wrong: **B** the LIS records and routes data but does not diagnose the patient; **C** accessioning does not delete the order; it links to it; **D** the physical specimen label is still required in addition to the LIS entry.

questions.stem: A specimen that requires body-temperature handling (e.g., a cold agglutinin sample) is collected. Which handling step preserves its integrity during transport?

options.text: Keep the specimen warmed to about 37 degrees Celsius using an approved warming device
Place it in crushed ice immediately
Freeze it solid for transport
Protect it from light in a freezer

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Cold-agglutinin and similar specimens must be kept warm at about 37 degrees Celsius with an approved warming device so the analyte does not change before testing. Why the others are wrong: **B** placing such a specimen on ice causes the cold agglutinins to bind and invalidates the result; **C** freezing is the opposite of the required warm handling; **D** the relevant requirement is warmth, not light protection or freezing.

questions.stem: Place the following preanalytical processing steps for a routine serum chemistry specimen in the correct order, from first to last (assume the tube is already collected, mixed, and labeled).

options.text: Allow the specimen to clot fully at room temperature
Centrifuge the tube to separate serum from cells
Transfer/aliquot the serum into a labeled tube if required
Store or transport the aliquot at the required temperature

questions.explanation: The blood must first clot fully (about 30 minutes at room temperature) so a clean clot forms; only then is the tube centrifuged to separate serum from cells. The serum is next transferred or aliquoted into a labeled tube if required, and finally stored or transported at the required temperature. Centrifuging before the clot forms produces fibrin and incomplete separation, and aliquoting must follow separation, so this order protects specimen integrity.

questions.stem: A clean-catch midstream urine specimen is ordered. What is the main reason for the clean-catch midstream technique?

options.text: To reduce contamination from skin and genital flora so the sample better reflects the urinary tract
To collect the largest possible volume
To make the urine appear clearer
To avoid the need to label the cup

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Cleansing and collecting midstream reduces contamination from surrounding skin and genital flora, so the specimen better represents the urinary tract for testing. Why the others are wrong: **B** the goal is a clean representative sample, not maximum volume; **C** the technique is about reducing contamination, not cosmetic clarity; **D** every specimen, including a clean-catch, still requires proper labeling.

questions.stem: A phlebotomist transports specimens between buildings. Which practice best maintains safety and specimen integrity in transit?

options.text: Carry tubes loose in a lab-coat pocket for convenience
Use a leak-proof, biohazard-labeled transport bag or container that keeps tubes upright and contained
Hold the tubes by hand and walk quickly
Place the tubes in a shirt pocket against the body for warmth

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A leak-proof, biohazard-labeled transport bag or container keeps tubes upright and contained, protecting both the specimen and anyone handling it. Why the others are wrong: **A** loose tubes in a pocket can break, leak, or be lost; **C** carrying tubes by hand risks dropping and breakage; **D** a shirt pocket against the body is unsafe, inappropriately warms the specimen, and risks contamination.

flashcards.back: Blood cultures (sterile) first, then light-blue (sodium citrate), then gold/red SST or red serum, then green (heparin), then lavender (EDTA), then gray (sodium fluoride/potassium oxalate). The order prevents additive carryover between tubes.

flashcards.front: Tube stopper colors and their additives
flashcards.back: Light-blue = sodium citrate (coagulation, 9:1 ratio); gold/red SST = clot activator + gel (serum chemistry); green = heparin (plasma chemistry); lavender = EDTA (CBC/hematology); gray = sodium fluoride/potassium oxalate (glucose/lactate).
Leave a tourniquet on no longer than one minute. Prolonged application causes hemoconcentration, falsely raising analytes such as proteins, potassium, and red cell counts.

The median cubital vein is preferred—large, well anchored, and away from major nerves and arteries. The cephalic vein is a second choice; the basilic vein is last because it lies near the brachial artery and median nerve.

Hemolysis is rupture of red blood cells within the specimen (often from a too-small needle, vigorous mixing, or forceful draw), falsely elevating potassium. A hematoma is blood leaking into tissue at the site, causing swelling and bruising—stop the draw and apply pressure.
Insert the needle at about 15 to 30 degrees, bevel up, following the vein's path. Too steep an angle risks puncturing the back wall of the vein.

Treat every patient's blood and body fluids as potentially infectious, regardless of diagnosis. Core elements include hand hygiene with every contact, appropriate PPE, safe sharps handling, and no recapping of needles.
Activate the needle's safety device and drop it immediately into a puncture-resistant sharps container at the point of use. Never recap (especially two-handed), bend, or break a contaminated needle.
Contact = gloves + gown. Droplet = surgical mask (plus eye protection). Airborne = N95 respirator + negative-pressure room. These are added on top of Standard Precautions for specific organisms.

HIPAA protects patients' protected health information. PHI may be used or disclosed without separate authorization for treatment, payment, and healthcare operations, following the minimum-necessary principle. A phlebotomist must not interpret results (outside scope of practice).

Use at least two patient-specific identifiers (e.g., full name and date of birth). Have the patient actively state them and match to the requisition and wristband. Room/bed number is never an acceptable identifier.

Requires rigorous skin antisepsis (e.g., chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine) to minimize skin-flora contamination and false positives. Culture bottles are always drawn first in the order of draw to maintain sterility.

Bilirubin and certain analytes must be protected from light (amber tube/foil) to prevent breakdown. Chilled specimens go in crushed ice or an ice-water slurry for even cooling—do not freeze whole blood, as it lyses cells.
